content: Preventing childhood obesity is a critical global public health priority due to its significant impact on both acute and chronic diseases, overall health, development, and well-being. The body of evidence supporting strategies to prevent obesity is extensive and continues to grow rapidly. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of various interventions, including dietary and physical activity components, or a combination of both, in preventing obesity in children. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed interventions targeting diet, physical activity, or both, in children aged 0 to 17 years. These studies reported outcomes at least 12 weeks after the baseline. Data were collected and analyzed independently by two authors, who assessed the risk of bias and evaluated the certainty of evidence using the GRADE framework. The primary outcomes analyzed were changes in BMI and zBMI, with separate meta-analyses conducted for three age groups: 0 to 5 years, 6 to 12 years, and 13 to 18 years. Findings for Children Aged 0 to 5 Years: Moderate-certainty evidence from 16 RCTs (n = 6,261) showed that combined diet and physical activity interventions reduced BMI (mean difference [MD] −0.07 kg/m², 95% confidence interval [CI] −0.14 to −0.01) and had a similar effect on zBMI (MD −0.11, 95% CI −0.21 to 0.01). Diet-only interventions (moderate-certainty evidence) and physical activity-only interventions (high-certainty evidence) did not significantly reduce BMI or zBMI in this age group. Findings for Children Aged 6 to 12 Years: Moderate-certainty evidence from 14 RCTs (n = 16,410) indicated that physical activity interventions reduced BMI (MD −0.10 kg/m², 95% CI −0.14 to −0.05). However, these interventions had little to no effect on zBMI (MD −0.02, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.02). Low-certainty evidence from 20 RCTs (n = 24,043) suggested that combined diet and physical activity interventions reduced zBMI (MD −0.05, 95% CI −0.10 to −0.01). High-certainty evidence showed that diet-only interventions had minimal impact on BMI (MD −0.02 kg/m², 95% CI −0.11 to 0.06) or zBMI (MD −0.03, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.01). Findings for Adolescents Aged 13 to 18 Years: Very low-certainty evidence from 4 RCTs (n = 720) suggested that physical activity interventions reduced BMI (MD −1.53 kg/m², 95% CI −2.67 to −0.39). Low-certainty evidence from 1 RCT (n = 100) indicated a reduction in zBMI (MD −0.2, 95% CI −0.3 to −0.1). Low-certainty evidence from 8 RCTs (n = 16,583) showed that combined diet and physical activity interventions had no significant effect on BMI (MD −0.02 kg/m², 95% CI −0.10 to 0.05) or zBMI (MD 0.01, 95% CI −0.05 to 0.07). Evidence from 2 RCTs (low-certainty; n = 294) found no effect of diet-only interventions on BMI. Direct Comparisons of Interventions: Two RCTs directly compared diet interventions with either physical activity or combined diet and physical activity interventions in children aged 6 to 12 years. These studies reported no significant differences between the intervention types. Adverse Effects and Health Inequalities: Where reported, interventions did not appear to cause adverse effects (16 RCTs) or exacerbate health inequalities related to gender (30 RCTs) or socioeconomic status (18 RCTs). However, relatively few studies specifically examined these factors. Conclusions: For children aged 0 to 5 years, combined diet and physical activity interventions can reduce the risk of obesity, as measured by BMI and zBMI. There is weaker evidence suggesting that diet-only interventions may also be beneficial, but physical activity-only interventions are not effective in this age group. For children aged 6 to 12 years and adolescents aged 13 to 18 years, physical activity-only interventions can reduce BMI, but there is no evidence that diet-only interventions are effective. Combined diet and physical activity interventions may have some effect in these age groups, but the evidence is less robust. Importantly, interventions to prevent childhood obesity do not appear to result in adverse effects or increase health inequalities. This review will not be updated in its current form. To better manage the growing number of RCTs on childhood obesity prevention, future updates will be divided into three separate reviews based on the age of the children.
